Terrible Devastation.
CLEVELAND, Aug. 9.—Reports continue to come in of widespread devastation by the recent storms in northern Ohio, which have been of unparalleled severity. A special from Wakeman says the storm there yesterday was accompanied by hail which cut down crops and gardens over a considerable extent of territory. Thirty bridges were swept away. In Holmes County the oat crop is totally destroyed, the potatoes nearly ruined, and corn greatly damaged. Whole farms on the hill sides are denuded of soil as well as crops. Decaying vegetable matter on the bottom lands has already become offensive, and is producing sickness. Barns in many places were struck by lightning and burned with their stores. Losses of this character are numerous, and very considerable in the aggregate.

[Special to the News and Courter.]

LANCASTER, August 9.—Hearing that a negro had been lynched last night near this place, your correspondent at an early hour this morning repaired to the scene, which is in a lonely spot about one and a half miles east of here. Arriving on the ground I found the body of a negro hanging from the limb of a small white oak tree with his toes touching terra firma. I gathered the following particulars: On Monday night, the 7th instant, Dan Blakeney, colored, who was employed as a farm hand by a prominent citizen of this county who lives fourteen miles east of this place, entered the room of the twelve-year old daughter of his employer and attempted to assault her. The screams of the child aroused the household and the villain fled without having accomplished his hellish purpose. He was pursued and captured and confessed everything. A posse of constables started to jail with the fiend, but when about two miles from Lancaster an engaged body of good citizens took fercible possession of Dan Blakeney and hung him to a convenient tree. That he met a just but terrible fate is the verdict of all, both white and colored.

Yesterday another negro was lodged in our county jail for committing a rape on a mulatto girl. Serious threats of lynching are being made by the colored people.

E. B. R.

THE RESULT IN ALABAMA.—The latest accounts from the recent State election in Alabama show the election of O'Neal and all the Democratic State ticket by a large majority, though much reduced from that of 1880. The election was very quiet and a light vote was polled everywhere. In the "black belt" the Republicans were not organized. Many negroes voted the Democratic ticket. In the northern part of the State the Republican-Independent-Greenback State ticket was successful in many counties. Calbert, Shulman, DeKalb, Elmore, Erowah, Laurence, Lauderdale, Limestone, Jackson, Madison and Morgan have elected Independents to the Legislature. In a number of counties the Democrats have been successful by only narrow majorities and in others the official count will be necessary to decide the result. The probabilities are that the Democratic ticket will not have more than 30,000 majority, and that there will be at least twenty Independents in the Assembly.

THE KEMPER HORROR.
The Outrage On, and Murder of, Mrs.
Callie Henson.
*THE BRUTE LYNCHED.
We have some further particulars of the late horrible crime in Kemper county and the subsequent lynching of the murderer, obtained from parties who reside in the vicinity of the occurrence. Mr. Aleck Henson was married last December to Miss Callie Echols, who was but 17 years of age and the daughter of Osborne Echols, a substantial farmer of Neshoba county. After marriage he settled on a farm in Kemper county, near the Neshoba line. On Thursday morning he left home early, taking his dinner with him, to plough on his farm, about a mile and a half from his residence. He returned late, and could see nothing of his wife. He called her but with no response, and finally, supposing she had gone to a neighbor's, started to look for her. A negro named George Hughes, who was a tenant on Henson's farm, and lived with his family in a cabin a few hundred yards from the house, came up to assist in the search, and as Henson was going off, told him to look in the well, that she might be there. The negro took a pole, put it in the well and cried out he had found her body. The well was eight or ten feet deep and full of water. Assistance was obtained and the dead body of Mrs. Henson was taken from the well. It was seen from examination of the body that she was first murdered and then thrown in the well. Her hair was dishevelled and there were marks of violence on her throat—the imprint of fingers by which she had been strangled. The right ear was bitten nearly off, and the impression made by four human teeth was clearly seen. An inquest was held on the body Friday morning before Isaac Dawes, Justice of the Peace, and after hearing all the testimony, there was no doubt that she came to her death from violence. Suspicion was directed towards the negro Hughes and he was arrested. The fact that he suggested she might have fallen into the well, his presence on the place after Mr. Henson left, the marks of violence, and many other circumstances pointed to his guilt. Among them was the fact that he had changed his clothes on Thursday, and when an effort was made to examine them it appears they had been washed by his wife. He had an examination before Esquire Dawes, which was not concluded until late Friday evening. He was ordered to be committed to jail, and Constable William Smith started with him to DeKalb, intending to take him there that night. About half a mile from where the trial was held, a crowd of about 75 persons took the prisoner from the officer and he was at once hung.

A diabolical deed was done in Western Kemper county on Thursday morning. Heck Hinson, a young man in the Terry settlement, had been married about last Christmas to a beautiful young wife, and they were living happily together until last Thursday morning. On that day he left his home to be gone all day. He never saw his wife alive again. Returning late, he missed her and was greatly troubled. He was about to go in search of her, when a negro man, a tenant, having his cabin near his residence, hinted that she might be in the well. The horrible suspicion aroused by the hint proved to be a terrible reality. The indications were that the negro had ravished her very soon after her husband had left her there alone to the tender mercies of a black demon. The breakfast table was standing as he left it to leave home after eating his breakfast, and the cow was yet unmilked, showing that the brute was in a hurry to accomplish his diabolical deed. He was put under arrest, and taken before the Justice of the district the next day. His guilt was established beyond a doubt, and a Kemper county mob promptly interposed and saved the officers of the law any further trouble about disposing of him. That is the way of the Kemper boys in dealing with devils in human form. Now, ye stalwart scoundrels, howl long, and loud, and make the most of it.—Meridian Mercury.

The people of the city of Racine were thrown into a state of unusual excitement on Friday night last by the shooting of one of their most prominent citizens, Capt. W. R. Pugh. Capt. Pugh was captain of the schooner Rainbow, and reputed to have been worth a considerable fortune. He was much respected by the community in Racine. It seems that a walking match took place on that evening at Belle City Hall between Higgie, of Racine, and one Dammars, of Chicago, Higgie winning the race; that Capt. Pugh and Hardy Clifford, of Milwaukee, wagered $175 on the race, Pugh betting on Higgie. After the affair was over Clifford refused to allow the stakeholder, Simpson, to pay the money he had bet and lost, at the same time accusing Capt. Pugh of having bought up the two men and roping him in. There was no truth in the matter and the captain informed him to that effect and most emphatically denied it. Clifford then sneaked off and went to the Huggins House, being a little worse off for liquor. Shortly after Capt. Pugh entered the private room at the hotel and asked Ed. Simpson, the stakeholder, for the money. Simpson refused to give it up, saying that Clifford had told him not to, but advised the captain to go up stairs and see Clifford about the matter. This he did, meeting Clifford in the office and asking him to come down stairs and settle the bill. He refused to go, but the captain good naturedly caught hold of his coat and led him to the head of the stairs, when he jerked away and without the least cause or provocation pulled a revolver from his pocket and fired at Capt. Pugh, but the shot struck the wall and did no harm. Pugh then jumped and caught hold of the murderous villain, as did Arthur Cressing, but he had murder in his heart and shot again, the bullet going into the floor. He then fired two more shots in quick succession, both taking effect. Pugh then descended the stairs and was taken to his home, where he died on Saturday morning. The excitement was intense. Capt. Pugh, though somewhat of a sporting man, was very popular and had many friends, not only in Racine but in Kenosha. Clifford gave himself up to the officers and was lodged in jail. So indignant were the people that an attempt was made to lynch him; the militia was ordered out for protection, and the preliminary examination before Justice Snyder took place in the residence of the Sheriff adjacent to the jail to avoid a disastrous result. The excitement died away during Monday, still a righteous indignation exists in the minds of the Racine people and many friends throughout the state, and even now Clindon may see to it that he does not get the unceremonious execution of the law, if not of statute law, a law which an indlgnant and injured people make for themselves. The procession was formed by the Racine Club, followed by the Knights of Pythias, and the Masonic lodge, of all which he was a member, and hundreds of citizens. The ceremonies at the grave were conducted according to the rites of the Free Masons.

A heavy volunteer guard has been kept around the jail day and night, both for the safe-keeping of the prisoners and to prevent anything like mob violence.

I see the Atlanta Post-Appeal, in a very recent issue, in an editorial article on the "Eastman Riot," attributes the trouble to the "drawing of the color line" by the whites. Such articles are apt to inflame the minds of the negroes and of the Northern people, and to injure not only the Democratic party, but to seriously affect the business interests of our people. Now, I happen to know that, if there was any such thing as drawing the color line, it was done by the negroes themselves. Their violence toward the whites generally, their cries of vengeance because, as they said, "one of their color had been killed," their brutal murder of an innocent white man, and threatening all our white citizens, show who it is that draws the color line. The negroes themselves do it, and they are the ones who keep it up.

ATLANTA, GA., September 7.—Last week negroes who had been engaged in a riot that occurred in Dodge county recently, were being tried. Indignation about Eastman is so great because all of the prisoners were not sentenced to be hung that the penitentiary guard had to steal away in the night with his captives. Jolly Colonel Jack Brown, brown and effervescent, has turned up in Washington again, and was to-day interviewed by one of the inquisitive reporters of THE CRITIC.

“Where’ve ye been, Kurnel?” THE CRITIC asked, adopting McKee Rankin’s old “49” dialect.

“I have been in Georgia for the past seven weeks.

“Politics down thar is boomin’, I ’spose ?”

“Yes, sir, everything in politics seems lovely; that is, the Democrats are weakening, and there is a strong probability of Stephens’ defeat for Governor. Independent Republicans and Greenbackers have united against bossism and ring Democracy, and we believe there will be such a change in the October and November elections as will astonish the nation. Many Republicans and anti-Bourbons will be elected to the Legislature, and there will be a change in our Congressional delegation.”

“You didn’t get the Congressional nomination, it appears,” THE CRITIC remarked seriocomically.

“No, I did not get the nomination for Congress in my district, but I did much better; that is, I succeeded in concentrating the entire Republican vote on Judge Harrell, the Independent anti-Bourbon candidate. The Judge is a man of good character, splendid ability, and for four years presided over the Superior Court of the Pataulo circuit. Hundreds of Democrats will vote for him; besides there are three thousand more Republican voters than Democratic in my District. My party is thoroughly organized and all its members will vote for Judge Harrell; hence I believe that the old Third will be represented by an anti-Bourbon in the Forty-eighth Congress.”

“You’ve been busy, then, during your absence?”
"You've been busy, then, during your absence?"
"Yes. Although I have done some good work for the past few weeks, yet I shall be on hand in October to render Judge Harrell all the assistance in my power."

Much time and money have been wasted on them. The idea of taking up the time of the Courts and country more than three months in trying one case is preposterous. Why, sir, I have defended more than sixty murderers since the 6th day of last August. I know it seems impossible, but it is, nevertheless, true as gospel. Most of the excursionists were drinking or drunk, as well as armed with pistols, knives or razors. About two p. m. of that day the marshal and his deputy of the village arrested one of their number for stealing a watch. While taking him to jail the prisoner attempted to escape and was killed.

"Finally two or three hundred of them espied a young man running away from the main street, and supposing him to be the Marshal fleeing from their threat and vengeance, they began chase at full speed, sending after the fugitive a hundred pistol balls, two or three of which took effect. The result of these trials was as follows: On Tuesday, the 17th of August, ten of the defendants were put on trial in one batch, viz: Ella Moore, Reddick Powell, Bob Donelson, Joe King, Simon O'Gwinn alias O'Quinn, Isaac Shipman, Henry Howell, Jack Knoles, John Kellam and Robert Stith. After a trial that lasted five days, these were all found guilty of murder in the second degree. The last four were recommended to life imprisonment in the penitentiary. The first six were sentenced by Judge Pate to explain the crime of which they were convicted upon the scaffold on the 20th of October, between the hours of 11 o'clock a. m. and 3 o'clock p. m., privately, in the town of Eastman, and in the meantime were sent to Bibb county jail for safe keeping. These were the strongest cases, and it is thought that among them is included the one who actually did the shooting that was the immediate cause of Mr. Harvard's death, while it is certain that they include those who took the most active part in the riot from its inception to its tragic end.

Then seven others charged and indicted for the same offense were put upon trial, to wit: Daniel Bryant, Robert, Robert, Gus Gibbs, Robert George, Robert, Best, James Oliver Copeland, Frank Adams, and William McRae. Their trial lasted four or five days, and the jury, after a searching investigation, rendered a verdict against all of the defendants for murder in the second degree, recommending them to imprisonment in the penitentiary for life. In the next and last batch there were five prisoners tried together, viz: Stafford Foster, Robert Parish, George Frink, Henry Carmichael and Jim Grlswold, with the same result as in the cases of the last preceding seven. In this case Judge Mershon presided for Judge Pate. The State was represented in the trials of the rioters by J. M. Stubbs of Dublin, Solicitor General Eason, J. F. DeLacy, E. Herrman, and Roberts & Smith, of Eastman. The defendants were represented by Colonel Jack Brown, of Americus; J. Bishop, Jr., of Eastman; J. W. Haygood, of Montezuma; Courtland Symmes, of Brunswick, and T. C. Taylor, of Hawkinsville. The investigations were long and tedious. The prisoners had a perfectly fair and impartial trial. But the evidence against them was strong, and could not be rebutted or overcome. Some of those who were sent to the penitentiary for life may well thank their stars that they were so fortunate as to save their necks. It is true, in the cases of two or three of those who were recommended to the mercy of the court and sentenced to the penitentiary, the evidence was mostly circumstantial, but the links in the chain of circumstances were strong and well connected. In all the cases but two or three, however, the testimony left no peg upon which to hang a reasonable doubt as to the guilt of the parties. The writer knows whereof he speaks, for he was present at the trials, connected with the cases as counsel for the defendants, and has a brief of the evidence now before him.

The August special term of the court, held for the purpose of trying the rioters, was an important as well as an expensive one to Dodge county. Besides the indictment and conviction of twenty-one men and one woman, six of whom, including the woman, for murder, were sentenced to death to answer for their crime, bills of indictment were also returned against J. B. A. Buchan and A. P. Harrell for manslaughter; and a large number of bills were found against parties for smaller offenses, amounting only to misdemeanors.

This special term of the court cost our county about $7,000 in extra taxes, besides the individual expenses and inconveniences to our citizens. For several weeks there was a stagnation in trade and business of every kind; farmers and business men from all parts of the county were called away from their homes to attend court as jurors and witnesses to the great neglect and suffering of their private affairs.

Since the court adjourned many of our citizens have been in constant suspense in anticipation of more trouble, owing to numerous wild rumors that have been circulated to the effect that the colored people intended to interfere with the course of law and justice, and make an attempt to prevent the execution of the six rioters convicted of murder and sentenced to be hanged. Even while the court was yet in session, Judge Pate received an anonymous postal card from Macon, signed "Somebody," and threatening his life. The Atlanta Defiance, a newspaper published by negroes, in its issue of September 19th, contained an editorial outrageously attacking the court and juries that tried the rioters, stating that they were convicting innocent colored men by the wholesale (all of which was unqualified false), and calling upon the colored people generally to know whether they would tamely submit to such a procedure. The Savannah Echo, another newspaper edited by negroes, copied this shameful article and gave it still further circulation. Again, recently, the Echo published another editorial in its own columns scurrillous in its character, and calculated to incite the negroes to some act of violence and interference with the verdict of the jury and order of the court convicting the rioters and sentencing them to be hung. A few days ago another anonymous postal card was mailed at the post office here, directed to "Mr. Everybody, By G—d, Eastman, Ga." and threatening trouble on the day of the hanging, saying that when those negroes are hung "we will all die together." There have also been various rumors of secret meetings held by the negroes, plotting to rescue the prisoners. Last week Sheriff Sapp received a letter from the jailer in Macon stating that he was informed that the negroes there were organized to prevent the prisoners from being brought down and executed; that it was rumored that an attempt would be made to rescue them between here and Macon, by tearing up the railroad track and wrecking the train upon which they were to be brought down, and that there would probably be a thousand negroes here on the day of the execution from Dodge's railroad in Telfair county, and other places, to play the mischief generally.

In view of all these things, for the protection and safety of our town, for the preservation of order, and to maintain the majesty of the law and carry out the mandates of the court, our citizens organized themselves into a quasi military company to assist the Sheriff in case he needed assistance; the Town Council was recommended to put several extra policemen on duty at night, and to put on a strong force on the day of the execution, and the Sheriff summoned a posse of a hundred and fifty or two hundred men from the county for guard duty to-day.

The crowd of darkles steadily increased in numbers, and they became more and more tumultuous. Sheriff Sapp saw that trouble was brewing, and that his own life was in imminent peril, for the negroes were already beginning to make threats and talk of revenge, saying that they had four men to one white man, and if they didn't take the advantage of it they ought to have their d—d throats cut.

Mr. Sapp therefore went out of town and remained away for several hours, for they were threatening to kill him, and doubtless would have done so had he not left when he did. The crowd grew larger and larger; the negroes became more and more bolsterous; the spark soon kindled into a flame that threatened every minute to burst forth like a fiery demon. The dead body of Jake Terrapin was removed to the platform in front of Sheriff Sapp's store, on County Road street, where a riotous mob rapidly gathered around it. The fury increased. There were loud cries for revenge because a colored man had been killed. A mob caught Harrell, the Deputy Marshal, near the post office, cut him severely with their knives, and would certainly have butchered him had not Mr. James Q. Harvard, a worthy young white man of Cochran, who happened to be in Eastman that day, passed by just at that untimely moment. By some means or other the attention of the mob was directed to him, and they were made to believe that he was the Marshal, and that they had the wrong man, as it seems that it was the Marshal and his deputy they wanted to kill. They immediately let Harrell go and went like so many bloodthirsty madmen after Mr. Harvard, chasing him several hundred yards with knives, clubs, brickbats, hatchets, pistols, etc., yelling and shooting and swearing vengeance every step of the way. Weary and breathless Mr. Harvard at length reached the residence of Mr. W. W. Harrell, on Fifth avenue, and rushing into the yard he ran under the house, feeling that he had found there a citadel of safety, for he could not believe the brutes in human form would violate the sanctity of the private home of a citizen who not only had absolutely nothing to do with the killing of their fellow creature, but at that time did not even know anything about the circumstances of the killing.

But here language is inadequate to picture what occurred. The scene fairly beggars description. An infuriated mob of two or three hundred colored people surrounded the premises. Flendish yells, terrible oaths, and, as witnesses afterwards swore, it seemed as though the discharge of a thousand pistols filled the air. Sticks and palings torn from the fence were waved in the air, brickbats were hurled into the hallway; the blades of knives and razors glistened in the sunlight; pistols were fired into and under the house; the gate and fence were pulled down. The mob demanded entrance into the house, but Mr. Harrell and his grandson, W. B. Daniel, stood at the gate and told them they had no right to enter his premises, and they must not do so. Then they threatened Mr. Harrell and Mr. Daniel, and swore they would go in; that the Marshal was in there and they intended to have him out or burn the house. The cursing grew louder and was accompanied by deafening shouts of "Burn the house! We will have him! Kill him!" After awhile several white men came up and did all in their power to quiet the disturbance and pacify the mob by reasoning with them and assuring them of assistance in aprehending the guilty party, if a crime had been committed; and when they seemed about to succeed in restoring quiet and order, a negro wench by the name of Ella Moore, the veriest devil in the crowd, would again arouse the passions of the mob and incite them on in their murderous enterprise by her wild gestures and frantic cries of "He killed my sister's child! The Eastman Hanging.
Yesterday there was enacted at Eastman, Dodge county, a scene which we believe has never been enacted before in Georgia, and let us devoutly hope may never have to be witnessed again. Five murderers—four men and one woman—were hung all at the same time to satisfy the just and stern demands of the law.

The crime for which these culprits suffered is fully detailed in all its horrible ghastliness in our telegraphic columns. It was indeed a bloody, cruel murder which these wretches, as ringleaders of a drunken and excited mob, caused to be committed upon the person of an innocent man against whom they, while inflamed with drink, had raised a cause less hue and cry. The outrageous crime would have amply justified the citizens of Eastman in taking the law in their own hands—if lynch law is ever justifiable—and making short work of the rioters and murderers on the spot. But, to the credit of those citizens be it spoken, they determined to let justice take its course. The offenders against the law were promptly arrested, fairly tried and duly sentenced in proportion to the enormity of their respective crimes. Fifteen were sent to the penitentiary—most of them for life—while six were found worthy of death.

Notwithstanding, too, that the condemned received fair trials, and the righteousness of their various sentences was not disputed, it was resolved by the Executive of this State that nothing should be left undone to mete out to them simple justice. To this end, although their counsel made no plea in their behalf after conviction, the Governor made it a special point to examine thoroughly into the evidence against them to see whether or not any extenuating circumstances existed which would justify executive clemency. After diligent investigation, however, the sentences of all save one were found to be richly deserved, and in the case of this one, Isaac Shipman, a reprieve was granted for thirty days. If, in the meantime, it be ascertained that there were any palliative conditions connected with his crime, his sentence will in all probability be commuted to imprisonment.

It will be seen, therefore, that the five criminals who yesterday suffered the extreme penalty of the law in Eastman were, notwithstanding the heinousness and horrible cold-bloodiness of their deed, granted every possible chance. They had forfeited their lives to the majesty of the law, and both justice and the well being of society demanded their execution. Their fate should be a lasting warning to the evil-minded and evil-disposed hereafter. It should teach all such that just so sure as they yield to passion and malice and commit crime, will their misdeeds be followed by punishment swift and stern, and throughout the length and breadth of Georgia crime is odious and law is supreme.

FOUR MEN AND A WOMAN HANGED. Paying the Penalty for their Share in a Riot from which Many Deaths Resulted.
EASTMAN, Ga., Oct. 20.—At 1 o'clock to-day Riddick Powell, Simon O'Guinn, Joseph King, Robert Donaldson, and Ella Moore, negroes, were hanged in the jail yard for murder and riot. No attempt was made to rescue them, and not more than fifty negroes, from whom violence was expected, were in the town. Military from Macon were present.

The crime they expiated was the flendish murder of a young white man named James Q. Harvard of Cochran, during a colored camp meeting at Eastman. On Sunday, Aug. 6, special trains were run to the camp from Macon and Jesup. The attendance of colored people was large, and a number of young white men were among the excursionists, including young Harvard. At the camp grounds the negroes indulged freely in whiskey and gambling. Among the sharpers who attended was Jake Johnson, a notorious character, who fleeced a number of the colored people, and took a watch and chain from one of them. The theft was reported to Marshal Buchan, who endeavored to arrest Jake, but the latter fled, and was pursued by the marshal and his deputy, Peter Harrell. Both fired shots at him, the deputy hitting and killing him instantly. The negroes became excited. They carried Jake's body to the camp grounds, where the women became loud in their lamentations and exclamations. Women and men were soon all wrought up to such a pitch of excitement that the men began to fire shots in the air. Suddenly in their frenzy they started to find Marshal Buchan and Deputy Harrell. In their search they saw a white man running through a grove of trees, and soon they were in hot pursuit. The man ran in the direction of the residence of W. W. Harrell, which he entered. The negroes surrounded the house, while five of them entered and secured James Q. Harvard, whom they mistook for the marshal's deputy. They took the young man from the house, and, tearing off pickets from the fence, beat him horribly. One placed a pistol at his head, and ended his agonies. Even after death the negroes continued to belabor the body.

They then went into the town in search of Marshal Buchan, but were met by the citizens, who had armed themselves. A fusillade was opened on both sides, but the negroes soon took to flight, not, however, before three of their number had been killed. Comparative quiet their trains. The homewai negroes boarded train was enlivened by numerous figures. The Shipman varying the disorder by stabbing his wife, and then, with a knife and pistol in his hands, daring the train officials to arrest him. The Sheriff of Dodge county succeeded in arresting ten negroes, including the woman Ella Moore, for the murder of young Harvard and participation in the riot, and the trial resulted in the conviction of six, five of whom paid the penalty of their crime on the scaffold to-day, the sixth. MONTGOMERY, ALA., March 24.—The mob made another demonstration Friday night, with a design to lynch the Moon brothers, in jail at Gadsden, but could not cross the river. St. Louis, June 27.—Yesterday morning Mrs. Low, the wife of a well known citizen of Flag Springs, Gentry county, near St. Joseph, committed suicide by cutting her threat with a razor. Cause, mental derangement. She was 55 years of age.

Hutter, while walking in the street with his wife, an Indian desperado named Francisco Tajaya, better known as Navajo Frank, threw a lariat around Hutter's neck, put spurs to his horse and rode of at a rapid rate, dragging the man over the rock street for a hundred yards or more. noah-parks-winston-county-1882-07-19.A10: A COLORED preacher of Mississippi has been lynched by his neighbors because "he stole corn." His offense justified the punishment. The peculiar and exclusive field of thieving operations of the negro minister is the hen-house. In a sense he is licensed to steal chickens, for the world recognizes the fact that the affinity of hens and negroes is something that cannot be overcome. It is popularly accepted as a truth that a black preacher can no more avoid prowling about henroosts than he can fly when the power to do so would be most advantageous to him. This being so the owners of hens are disposed to bottle their wrath at the loss of fowls when they are aware of the proximity of a colored minister. When one of these dispensers of the gospel becomes so immoral as to stray from his natural and recognized field of operations, and steals corn, there seems no other course left than to promptly lynch him.

MRS. ABRAHAM LINCOLN died at Springfield, Illinois, July 16. Mrs. Lincoln had a great sense of wrong, not only in the loss of her husband, but in the treatment she has received from the world since that event. She spent a good deal of time in Europe in a wandering, aimless way, seeking impossible health and consolation for cureless wounds. simon-woods-bayou-cocodrie-1882-05-16.A5: Simon Woods, a colored desperado, was killed by deputy sheriff E. A. McKinney, at Wilson's sawmill on Bayou Cocodrie, about 8 o'clock last Tuesday evening. Woods, by his own statement, was a refugee from the parish of St. Martin, where he had committed some crime. He was in jail here last year for carrying concealed weapons. Not long since he took away from one Anderson Stewart, another colored man living at Wilson's sawmill, his thirteen year year old daughter. A few daws ago the girl's mother got her her back home. Woods came there, threw the mother down, and was was attempting to cut her throat with a knife, when Stewart knocked or pulled him off. Woods then "went for him," but he he escaped into house and fastened the doors against him. He made violent efforts to break in, with threats to kill, ect., but was finally persuaded to desist and go away. Steward came to Opelousas last Tuesday, and made an affidavit against Woods; and he would not return home until an officer was sent to arrest Woods, and he advised that more than two men be sent to make the arrest, as Woods had sworn that he would not be arrested by the sheriff nor anybody else, and that he would be certain to kill at least two men with the double barrel gun which he carried. Woods waited at Stewart's cabin for him to return, threatening that he would kill him. When deputy sheriff McKinney arrived there Tuesday, Stewart retired to the woods with his gun. He was told that he could not capture him with a pistol, whereupon he procured a gun; and to induce Woods, who was no doubt watching near by, to come in from the woods, McKinney changed clothes with some one at the mill, and went to work in his place, while he mounted McKinney's horse and rode off. This strategem had the desired effect. Woods came to the mill office, set his gun down, and stated to those present that he wanted this matter (between Stewart and himself) settled. McKinney who was behind the building, made his appearance, and informed Woods that he was his prisoner. Woods sprang to his gun and seized it. McKinney told him to keep his hands off the gun, or he would shoot him. This having no effect, he covered Woods, and as he jerked up his gun he fired. Woods fell mortally wounded, the entire charge of shot making one hole through his body, on one side about the lower ribs. When he fell both barrels of his gun were found cocked. Woods died before morning. The verdict of the coriner's jury was justifyable homicide.

Opelousas, Parish of St. Landry, La., May 20, 1882.
KILLED.—On Tuesday evening, the 16th inst., deputy sheriff E. A. McKinney went to Wilson's saw-mill, about twenty-four miles northwest of Opelousas, to arrest a celored man, by the name of Simon Woods, charged with horse stealing, and assault and battery. Upon his arrival there, Mr. Wilson warned him of the desperate character of the negro, who, he said, was armed with a double barrel shot gun, and had threatened to kill any man who would attempt to arrest him. McKinney changed clothes with one of the workmen at the mill, so that the accused might not recognize him and make his escape. The man who had changed clothes with McKinney rode off as though coming to town, while McKinney took his place at work at the mill to await the expected arrival of Woods. In the meantime he had secured a shot gun to protect himself, in case the negro should attempt to use his gun in resisting arrest. Late in the evening, Woods made his appearance armed with a shot gun and evidently expecting the arrival of an officer to arrest him. McKinney approached him, and asked if he was Simon Woods. He replied that he was. McKinney then said to him, "I have a warrant to arrest you, and you are my prisoner." Woods picked up his gun, when McKinney leveled his gun at the same time, and told him to drop his gun or he would shoot him. But instead of heeding the warning, Woods cocked both barrels of his gun and commenced raising it to his shoulder. McKinney fired just in time to save his own life, shooting Woods in the bowels, from which wound he died the next morning. Before dying, he stated that the officer had done right in shooting him; because he was determined not to be arrested, or go to jail again. Woods had been in this parish for two years, and was a fugitive from St. Martin parish, where he escaped from jail, under a charge of stabbing a man with intent to murder. He was said to be a dangerous and desperate character.

A Rare Villain.
Last Thursday, 9th instant, a white man who has been traveling through the County selling garden seed, was in No. 6 Township. He went to a gentleman's plantation and asked a negro on the place if the gentleman was at home. Being told that he was not, he said that he would not go to the house. But he did go. He knocked at the door, and the lady came to the door and opened it. The fellow there used the most insulting language to her. She slammed the door in his face; but he opened it and walked in. She fled into the kitchen in the back part of the house. He pursued her there, and she fled out of the house and into the house of a colored family near by. The fellow then left. When the husband came home at night and heard of the affair he was, of course, very angry; and, with some of his neighbors started out early Friday morning after the fellow. Had they caught him he would have fared badly. After riding about fifty miles they returned, and telegraphed to Laurens for the arrest of the fellow if found. He was arrested at Laurens and brought down on the train Saturday morning and placed in jail. He says he is from Buncombe County, North Carolina, and that his name is Spain.

Saturday there were threats of lynching, but wise counsels prevailed and everything became quiet. Monday evening it began to be whispered about that Spain would be taken from the jail. From what can be learned it was the intention to take him out, give him a decent threshing and turn him loose. The Sheriff getting wind of the matter called out a posse to guard the jail, and thus frustrated the plan. When everything had become quiet, and the crowd had dispersed, Trial Justice Fair, upon whose warrant Spain had been committed, sent an order of release to the Sheriff, and Spain was turned out. When released he did not tarry, but left at the top of his speed, and has not since been heard from.

A Young Wife Brutally Shot by a Hired Man.
Mrs. Joseph Copeland, of Hopedale, O., the Victim—The Murderer Confesses His Guilt—Threats of Lynching, But Better Counsel Prevails and He Will
BE PERMITTED TO PULL HEMP.
Special Dispatch to the Register.

HOPEDALE, O., August 31.—This staid and quiet little village was thrown into a fever of excitement by a telegram stating that a former resident of the vicinity had been murdered a few hours before.

The facts, as understood by your correspondent, are as follows: Mr. and Mrs. Joseph Copeland having linked their destinies, moved to Kewanee, Coles county, Illinois, for the purpose of locating, which they did some three or four years ago.

They visited friends here last winter, and upon their return were accompanied by a Mr. T. C. Bell, an old neighbor, and a young man by the name of Sylvester Machinson, he going for the purpose of finding employment, which he did a few days after their arrival.

A few days ago Mr. Copeland and Mr. Bell were called away on business, and upon their return found the body of Mrs. C. in the yard, mangled and bleeding, with two bullet holes in her breast and a severe cut on the forehead, supposed to have been made by a heavy instrument.

The object of the murderer was evidently to obtain money, eighty dollars belonging to Mr. Bell having been taken. Suspicion at once centered upon young Machinson as the guilty one, and he was arrested and the money and a revolver, with two empty chambers, were found upon his person.

The body of the victim was brought here yesterday and laid to rest in a neighboring cemetery, amid a host of sorrowing friends.

Further Particulars.

The Enquirer publishes the following additional facts in regard to the murder: At Kewanee, a farm hand who had been at work in that locality called at a farm house in the neighborhood. Here he found a lady alone, and after some delay he brutally murdered her by blows and by pistol shots, robbed the house of some money and departed, but some hours later joined in the search for the murderer, the body of the murdered lady having been found. He was subsequently arrested on suspicion, and finally on Monday confessed his crime. The discovery of this atrocity, together with the arrest and confession of the murderer, happening at the same time as the discovery and arrest of the bank robbers, naturally has given Kewanee an excitement that rarely falls to the lot of a rural town.

The examination of Makinson, the murderer of Mrs. Copeland, was held this forenoon. He waived examination and pleaded guilty, and was remanded to the county jail. Fully five thousand men were on the streets at an early hour this morning, determined that Makison should be hung before he left the place, but by the exertions of some of the, best citizens, coupled with the assurance of State's Attorney Gilchrist that the law should be fully carried out, he was allowed to be taken by the officers to the county jail.

An hour from the time he was removed it would have been impossible to have taken him from the court room without the citizens having taken him in charge and hanged him on the spot. Before taking him to the court room he made a full confession of the crime and gave all the particulars, telling where the stolen property was concealed, which was found as he described. No attempt to violate the person of Mrs. Copeland was made. He claims that he can give no explanation why he did the deed, as Mrs. Copeland was a good friend to him and had been very kind to him many times. Before being taken from the jail to the Court-room for examination he begged the officers to allow the crowd to hang him immediately, he wishing to die as soon as possible. Makison's confession was secured by a Pinkerton detective who was locked up in the same cell with him, and who made Makison believe he was Welch, the bank robber. A mutual interchange of confidence led to a full disclosure by the murder of all the details of his awful crime. Makison was taken to Cambridge Jail this afternoon, some twenty miles away, and there confined. He was willing to be handed over to the mob, saying that he knew he should be hung anyhow, and wanted to have it over at once.

EDITORIAL ITEMS.
Choctaw and Lawrence counties have no retail saloons.
Two hundred pupils attend the free schools at Kosciusko.
Mutilated coin is worth $1.00 per ounce, troy, in sums of $3.00.
The President has appointed Senator A. A. Sargent as Minister to Berlin.
O'Leary and Downey commence another walking match in New Orleans, Saturday.
A bill is before the Ohio Legislature to prevent and punish "treating" on election days.
The Atlanta branch of the Methodist Book Concern is to be discontinued. It doesn't pay.
A man named Brown was killed while attempting to get on a train at Gallman last Saturday.
The Natchez Theological Seminary, for colored people, has three hundred and thirty-five students.
Statistics show that there are 63,000 insane persons in the United States, or one to every 777 of population.
The Nihilists on trial at St. Petersburg number two dozen. Many of them are accused of more than one offence.
Thirty-one Americans are students at the Academy of Arts in Munich. Only the Germans outnumber them.
A little daughter of Wm. Wilson, near Woodville, was burnt to death, on the 25th inst., while playing with fire in a field.

The wife of the great statesman, Daniel Webster, died at New Rochelle, Mass., on the 27th ult. She was Webster's second wife.

The Corinth papers are still quarrelling. It is time they were dwelling together as brothers. Their quarrel is not interesting.

Blaine delivered an address in Washington, last Monday, on the life, services and death of Garfield. He had an immense audience.

Chicago has now a cable street railroad. The cars run without horse to steam attached, go quick and stop readily when wanted.

Senator Ben Hill has submitted to another surgical operation. This time on the glands of the throat. The report of the case is favorable.

Several Democratic members of the Senate put themselves to the trouble to deny that they have any collusion with the Blaine movement.

Jackson has been unsuccessful in securing amusements this year: Both Herman and Rice's Surprise Party cancelled their Jackson dates. The place did not lose much.

A rumor that Miss Ida Farrell, of Peoria, Illinois, is the recipient of much attention on the part of President Arthur, is creating a great flutter in social circles of Peoria.

It is said we are now importing from two or three thousand tons of potatoes a week, from Great Britain and Germany, besides cabbages, sauer-kraut, turnips, celery and carrots.

SULLIVAN has challenged Ryan to meet him in a boxing-match. Ryan says he yet intends to fight Sullivan in the ring and whip him. There are plenty of people who believe that he can do it.

An old fraud, purporting to be named Dr. C. M. Bell, of Baltimore, has succeeded in swindling many Southern publishers. We have evidence to prove that he is a thief and a swindler. Pass him around.

A man in Chicago, named Andrew Oleson, tried whisky as a remedy for small-pox, and drank five pints within the period of two hours. The remedy proved fatal before the disease had time to develop seriously.

The steamer Bertie Claiborne was burned near Vicksburg, last Thursday. Three children and a negro were drowned, and most of the cargo was consumed, the principal part being one hundred and sixty bales of cotton.

A CORRESPONDENT of the Clarion says: "Four years ago, in a communication to the Clarion, I expressed it as my opinion that the lien law had damaged the material interests of Mississippi more than the liberation of the slaves, and I still think so.'

WASHINGTON, April 25th.—In the Senate this afternoon, on motion of Miller of California, who reported it, the House bill to execute certain treaty stipulations relating to the Chinese was taken up, and the Senate committee amendments, up to the last sections (14 and 15) were agreed to as read.

By a vote of 32 noes against 26 ayes the Foreign Relations Committee amendment was rejected, which proposed to strike out the fourteenth section. This section prohibits Chinese naturalization.

The vote was as follows:

Ayes—Aldrich, Allison, Anthony, Blair, Conger, Davis of Illinois, Dawes, Frye, Hale, Harrison, Hawley, Hosr, Ingalls, Kellogg, Lapham, McDill, McMillan, Miller of New York, Morrill, Platt, Plumb, Rollins, Saunders, Thayer, Vanwyck and Windom—26.

The committee amendment striking out the fifteenth section, which defines the words "Chinese laborers," whenever used in the Act, to mean both skilled and unskilled laborers and Chinese employed in mining, was carried by a vote of ayes 29, noes 28.

The vote was a party one, except that Miller of California, Jones of Nevada, and Cameron of Wisconsin, voted "no" with the Democrats, and Davis of Illinois voted "aye" with the Republicans.

A Step in the Direction of a Civil Pension List.

NEW YORK, April 25th.—A Washington special says: The Commerce Committee today agreed to report favorably the bill to retire Edward A. Hillyer, a District Judge of the District of Nevada, with full pay during his natural life. He is afflicted with softening of the brain. More than local interest attaches to this bill, as in providig for the payment of full salary during his natural life, it takes a step in the direction of a civil pension list, which has always met with sturdy opposition from Congress and the people of the country.

Steamer Burned—Nine Lives Lost.

JACKSONVILLE (Fla.), April 25th.—The steamer City of Sanford, on the way here from Sanford, took fire yesterday morning, and nine persons—probably more—perished. The names of those actually known to be dead are as follows: Mrs. Oscar Keep and child, of Jacksonville, Fla.; Mrs. Ireland and daughter, of Como; Capt. S. H. Dawner, of Norwalk, Fla.; Capt. S. H. Artelle, of the schooner Magnolia (recently lost on Mosquito Lalat bar); Charles Pierce, and a nephew, Willie Brooks, a son of the pilot of the ill-fated steamer Dorsey. The steamer Bird, coming down the river a few miles ahead of the Sanford, put back and brought the survivors here. The steamer and contents are a total loss, nothing whatever being saved.

The Southern Cyclone.

MACON (Ga.), April 25th.—A cyclone passed through Smiggs and Jones counties Saturday night, a tract 800 yards wide being swept clean. Samuel Grove, the father of Samuel F. Grove, ex-member of Congress, was killed.

WILMINGTON (N. C.), April 25th.—A tornado crossed this State Saturday night, mowing a swath through the timber. One church, two sawmills, and a large number of dwellings were destroyed. One child was killed, and several persons seriously hurt.

PHILADELPHIA, April 25th.—McIlvain Bros.' drug and spice mill was damaged by fire to the extent of $40,000.

NEW YORK, April 25th.—The furniture storage warehouse of Geo. C. Flint & Co., 303 West street, was burned to-day, Loss, $75,000; partly insured.

TORONTO, April 25th.—A fire to-day destroyed the Parkdale round-house of the Credit Valley Railroad, and four locomotives were burned, Loss, $50,000.

The losses are small to individuals, none running over $10,000, but there are a large number of them.

WASHINGTON, April 25th.—In the election cases in the House to-day every man elected as a Greenbacker or Independent voted with the majority of Republicans, and it may be conceded that the Election Committee will be generally sustained by a majority of 10 to 12.

GEORGETOWN (O.), April 25th.—William Strull, recently discharged from the employment of Collins Summers, a prominent farmer near here, shot Mrs. Summers six times with a revolver Sunday evening, killing her instantly. The deed was done because Strull thought his victim caused his dismissal. This is the man who was corralled near Franklin, Pa., this afternoon, and who shot himself to prevent lynching.

A Vile Murderer Kills Himself.
CLEVELAND, April 25.—A Herald special from Canton states that about sunrise this morning William Stull, the Georgetown murderer, was cornered in some dense woods near New Franklin, fourteen miles southeast of Canton, by the Columbiana county sheriff and a posse of deputies, who had been following him since Sunday. Finding escape impossible he drew his revolver, with which he murdered Mrs. Sommers, and fired two shots into his head in quick succession, producing instant death. The excitement is intense in Stark and Columbiana counties.

The particulars of the vile wretch's most cowardly and revolting crime are as follows: Collins Summers, one of the most prominent farmers of Columbiana county, has had a hired hand named Wm. Stull in his employ for the past year or two; about ten days ago he discharged him on account of his quarrelsome disposition and since that time Stull has been lurking in the neighborhood. Late on Sunday Mrs. Summers was at the barn, milking her cow, when she saw Stull approaching, little dreaming of his murderous intent or of the horrible fate which awaited her. He came and stood within a few feet of Mrs. Sommers and said "Good evening." She noticed nothing wrong in his behavior, and, after answering him very pleasantly, resumed her work. Scarcely had she turned her back, when her cowardly assin deliberately drew his six shooter revolver and emptied the contents of all the chambers in the body of his innocent and defenceless victim, two of the balls taking a fatal effect, one in her breast and the other through her spine. The inhuman monster then fled, and the family were horified, on rushing to the barn, to behold the victim of the wretch weltering in her own gore. Stull accused Mrs. Summers as being instrumental in having him discharged, and this was the trivial pretext for his murdering her in cold blood.

Murder and Suicide.
Last Sunday morning, William Stull, a farm-hand who had been working for Collins Summers, near North Georgetown, Columbiana county, but discharged a few weeks previously, went to the barn where Mrs. Summers was milking, and after bidding her good morning, drew a revolver and fired five shots at her, one striking her in the back, hitting the spinal column, causing paralysis of the lower part of the body; a second took effect back of the left armpit, running around to the breast bone. The third struck her just above the knee. The murderer fled and was tracked to the neighborhood of Osnaburg by the officers, and on Tuesday morning the Sheriff of Columbiana county and six deputies caught sight of him in the woods near New Franklin, and surrounded him. Finding escape impossible, he drew the same revolver that did the shooting, placed it to his forehead, pulled the trigger and fell, dying in a few moments. He was barely 23 years old, and bore a grudge against Mrs. Summers, as he thought she had secured his discharge from the farm. Mrs. Summers is lying in a critical condition.
